3490:
To convene means to come together as a group for a formal, organized meeting — or to cause such a gathering to happen.

That's the heart of it. But there's more texture to it than a simple definition captures, so let's unpack it fully.

This is the most important thing to understand: "convene" works in two directions.

Direction 1 — A group comes together on its own:
Here, the subject is the group, and they are doing the assembling.

  • "The jury convened to reach a verdict."
  • "Parliament convened after the summer recess."
  • "The board of directors convened on Monday morning."

In these sentences, the group itself is gathering. No one is explicitly calling them together — we're simply describing the act of them assembling.

Direction 2 — Someone calls a group together:
Here, a person or authority with power causes the meeting to happen.

  • "The president convened an emergency cabinet meeting."
  • "The judge convened the court."
  • "The committee chair convened a special session."

In these sentences, one person is actively summoning or organizing others into a gathering.

Both usages are equally correct and equally common. The word "convene" comfortably handles both.
What Makes "Convene" Different from Just "Meet" or "Gather"

This is crucial. You could say "the team met" or "the team convened" — so what's the difference?

"Convene" carries three built-in assumptions that ordinary words like "meet" or "gather" do not:

1. Formality. When people convene, the gathering has an official, structured character. It's not a casual hangout, a friendly lunch, or a spontaneous chat. Courts convene. Committees convene. Parliaments convene. You would never say "my friends and I convened at the café" — that sounds strange because the setting is too informal. "Convene" implies an assembly that has rules, a purpose, an agenda, or an authority behind it.

2. A defined group with a shared role. The people who convene aren't random individuals — they are members of something: a council, a committee, a court, an assembly, a board. They share a formal role or function that gives them reason to be in that room together.

3. A serious purpose. People don't convene to have fun. They convene to deliberate, decide, investigate, legislate, negotiate, or judge. There is always a reason — and usually an important one — that justifies calling the group together.

So while "meet" is neutral and everyday, "convene" signals gravity, structure, and official purpose.

You'll most naturally encounter "convene" in these settings:

  • Legal and judicial: "The court will convene at 9 a.m." / "The grand jury convened to hear evidence."
  • Political and governmental: "Congress convened for an emergency session." / "World leaders convened at the summit."
  • Organizational and corporate: "The board convened to vote on the merger." / "A task force was convened to address the crisis."
  • Academic and institutional: "An expert panel convened to review the findings." / "A conference convened in Geneva."
  • International and diplomatic: "The UN Security Council convened an urgent meeting."

Notice the pattern: these are all high-stakes, structured, official situations.

When someone convenes a meeting (Direction 2), it's rarely just any random person doing so. Typically, it's someone with the authority, power, or recognized role to call that group together — a chairperson, a judge, a president, a secretary-general. This is why "convene" often implies not just a gathering, but one that was authorized or legitimized by someone in charge.

For example: "The UN Secretary-General convened an emergency session" tells you not only that a meeting happened, but that the person with the power to call it did so — which itself carries weight and news value.

Certain words naturally travel with "convene" in real usage. Getting familiar with these will help you sound natural:

  • Convene a meeting — the most common pairing
  • Convene a session — especially for courts, legislatures, councils
  • Convene a summit — for high-level international gatherings
  • Convene a panel / committee / commission — for investigative or advisory bodies
  • Convene urgently / in emergency — emphasizing the seriousness
  • Convene at [a location or time] — "The assembly convened at noon."
  • Be convened by [someone] — passive form: "The inquiry was convened by the minister."

• Present: "The committee convenes every quarter."
  • Past: "The court convened at dawn."
  • Future: "The council will convene next Tuesday."
  • Passive: "An emergency meeting was convened by the director."
  • Continuous: "The panel is convening to discuss the new regulations."
A Quick Contrast with Similar Words

WordHow it differs from "convene"
MeetCasual or formal, no implication of structure or authority
GatherUsually informal; can apply to objects, crowds, or people without structure
AssembleClose to "convene" but broader — can be informal or non-purposive (e.g., a crowd assembles)
SummonFocuses on the commanding act of calling someone; stronger sense of obligation
CongregatePeople coming together, often in large numbers, but not necessarily for a formal purpose

If you had to hold just one sentence in your head, let it be this:

"Convene" means to formally bring people together for an organized, purposeful gathering — or for that group to come together in such a manner.

Every time you see or hear "convene," ask yourself: Who is gathering? For what formal purpose? And who called them together? Answer those three questions, and you'll always fully understand the word in context.
3491:
Convenience means the quality of being easy, effortless, and without trouble. Something has convenience when it fits smoothly into your life — saving you time, effort, or difficulty.

Think of it this way: when something is hard to do, you struggle. When something has convenience, you don't struggle at all. It just... works, easily.

"Convenience" works in three slightly different ways depending on the sentence, but they all share the same root idea — ease and lack of difficulty.

Meaning 1 — The State or Quality of Being Easy

Here, "convenience" refers to an abstract quality — the property of something being easy, accessible, or hassle-free.

"I chose this apartment for its convenience — the supermarket, the bus stop, and the pharmacy are all within walking distance."

"Online banking offers great convenience because you don't have to visit a physical branch."

In these sentences, convenience isn't a thing you can touch. It's a quality — the characteristic of something being easy and saving you effort.

Meaning 2 — A Thing That Makes Life Easier

Here, "convenience" (or more often its plural, "conveniences") refers to a specific object, service, or feature that reduces effort and makes life more comfortable.

"A washing machine is a modern convenience."

"The hotel room came with all the conveniences — a microwave, a coffee maker, and fast Wi-Fi."

Here, the word shifts from an abstract quality to a concrete thing. The washing machine is a convenience because it exists to save you effort. Any device, service, or feature that removes difficulty from your life can be called a convenience.

Meaning 3 — A Suitable or Comfortable Time

This meaning is mostly found in fixed phrases and refers to a time that suits you — when something is easy or possible for you to do.

"Please call me back at your convenience." (= Call me whenever it suits you, whenever you have time.)

"At your earliest convenience, could you send me the report?" (= As soon as it is easy and possible for you to do so.)

"The documents will be ready for signing at your convenience."

In these expressions, "convenience" means the moment when doing something won't be difficult, rushed, or uncomfortable for you. It's a polite, formal way of saying "whenever works for you."

These are fixed phrases you'll encounter regularly. Knowing them will help you recognise convenience in the wild.

"For your convenience" — This phrase means "to make things easier for you." You'll often see it on signs, websites, and in customer service:
"For your convenience, our store is open 24 hours."
"For your convenience, you can pay online."

"For the sake of convenience" — This means doing something in the easiest or simplest way, even if it isn't perfect:
"For the sake of convenience, let's just order pizza instead of cooking."

"Convenience store" — A small shop that stays open late (sometimes all night) and sells everyday items like snacks, drinks, and household basics. It's called a "convenience store" because it is conveniently available when regular shops are closed.

"Convenience food" — Food that is very quick and easy to prepare, like instant noodles or frozen meals. It prioritises ease over quality or nutrition.

"A marriage of convenience" — This is an expression (not just about marriage) meaning an arrangement made for practical benefit rather than genuine feeling or true suitability:
"Their business partnership was a marriage of convenience — they didn't like each other, but they needed each other's resources."

"At your earliest convenience" — A polite, formal phrase meaning "as soon as you are able to, without it being difficult for you." It is softer than saying "as soon as possible" and is common in professional emails.
An Important Nuance: Convenience Can Have a Slight Negative Shadow

While "convenience" is usually a positive word, it sometimes carries a subtle negative implication — suggesting that something was done for the sake of ease rather than care, effort, or principle.

"He only apologised for convenience — he didn't actually mean it."

"The rules were changed for the government's convenience, not the public's benefit."

In these cases, "convenience" suggests that someone chose the easy path instead of the right or thoughtful one. So the word can carry a faint sense of laziness, self-interest, or compromise, depending on the context.

When you pluralise the word, it almost always refers to specific things that make life easier (Meaning 2 above):

"The house lacked modern conveniences — there was no central heating or hot water."

"Travellers in that era had few conveniences — no GPS, no mobile phones."

The plural is rarely used for Meaning 1 (the abstract quality) or Meaning 3 (a suitable time).

"Convenience" is ultimately about one idea: reducing difficulty in human life. Whether it describes the abstract quality of something being easy, a physical object that saves effort, or a phrase that means "whenever suits you," it always points to the same thing — the absence of struggle, the presence of ease.

When you see or hear "convenience," ask yourself: What difficulty is being removed here? Whose life is being made easier, and how? That question will always unlock the correct meaning.
3492:
Something is convenient when it fits your needs smoothly — it saves you time, effort, or trouble. It works well for you, right where and when you need it, without causing problems or requiring extra work.

When something is convenient, life becomes a little easier because of it. When it is not convenient, things feel awkward, poorly timed, or unnecessarily difficult.
What "Convenient" Describes

Places and locations

A place is convenient when it's easy to reach — nearby, accessible, not requiring extra travel.

  • "The grocery store is convenient — it's just around the corner from my house."
  • "The hotel is in a convenient location, close to the airport and the city center."

Times and scheduling

A time is convenient when it suits your schedule — when you're free, available, and don't need to rearrange other things.

  • "Is 3 PM a convenient time for you to meet?"
  • "I'll call you whenever it's convenient for you."

A convenient time is not forced or rushed. It fits naturally into your day.

Objects and tools

Something is convenient when it's designed in a way that makes a task easier or quicker.

  • "The bag has a convenient side pocket for your phone."
  • "The app has a convenient search feature that saves me a lot of time."

Methods, arrangements, and situations

A situation or arrangement is convenient when it removes effort and complication from your life.

  • "Online banking is very convenient — I can pay bills from home."
  • "Having a car is convenient when you live far from public transport."
The Key Feeling the Word Captures

"Convenient" captures the idea of ease without friction. When something is convenient:

  • You don't have to go out of your way
  • It fits your schedule, location, or needs naturally
  • It reduces effort
  • It doesn't create new problems for you

Think of it as a good fit between what you need and what exists. The better the fit, the more convenient something is.
"Convenient for" vs "Convenient to"

Both are correct, but they work a little differently.

Convenient for [a person] — good for that person's situation or needs:

  • "Tuesday works well — it's convenient for me."
  • "Is this location convenient for everyone?"

Convenient to [do something / a place] — easy to do, or close to a place:

  • "It's convenient to pay online rather than going to the bank."
  • "The station is convenient to the shopping area." (= it's close to it)
Degrees of Convenience

Like most adjectives, "convenient" comes in degrees:

  • "It would be more convenient if the office were closer."
  • "This is the most convenient option for us."
  • "A supermarket nearby would be very convenient."
  • "It's not particularly convenient, but I can manage."
The Opposite: Inconvenient

The opposite of convenient is inconvenient — something that causes difficulty, disruption, or extra effort.

  • "The meeting at 6 AM is very inconvenient for people who commute far."
  • "Moving the furniture today would be inconvenient — I'm expecting guests."

Understanding inconvenient sharpens the meaning of convenient: convenience is the absence of unnecessary trouble.
"Convenient" vs Similar Words

These words are close in meaning but are not the same.

Easy — focuses on how difficult something is

  • "The test was easy." (= not hard)
  • Convenient focuses on how well something fits your situation, not just on difficulty. Something can be easy to do but inconvenient (e.g., a task is simple but requires you to travel far). Something can also be convenient but not easy (a nearby hospital is convenient even though surgery is not easy).

Handy — easy to use, or nearby and useful; more informal, often about small objects

  • "A Swiss Army knife is handy on a camping trip."
  • Convenient is broader. It covers places, times, and situations — not just tools.

Practical — sensible, workable, and effective in real life

  • "A small car is practical for city driving."
  • Practical is about whether something makes good sense to use. Convenient is about whether it reduces your effort and fits your situation.

Accessible — possible to reach or use, often about physical or structural availability

  • "The building is accessible for wheelchair users."
  • Accessible is about whether you can reach or use something. Convenient is about how easily and comfortably it fits your needs — it implies the positive experience of something being well-placed or well-timed.
Common Word Pairings (Collocations)

Certain words naturally go together with convenient:

  • Conveniently located — "The café is conveniently located near the train station."
  • Convenient time / moment — "Please come at a convenient time."
  • Convenient for someone — "Is this convenient for you?"
  • At your convenience — "Reply at your convenience." (= whenever suits you; no rush)
  • For your convenience — "The form is available online for your convenience." (= to make things easier for you)
  • Convenient option / choice — "Online payment is a convenient option."
  • Find it convenient — "Many people find it convenient to shop online."
"For Your Convenience" — A Common Phrase

You will see this phrase often in formal writing, notices, and service contexts. It means: "We have done this to make things easier for you."

  • "For your convenience, the help desk is available 24 hours a day."
  • "Parking is available on-site for your convenience."

It signals that someone has made an effort to reduce the effort required from you.
A Subtle Use: Sarcasm and Suspicion

In spoken English especially, "convenient" can be used with a sarcastic or suspicious tone — implying that something is suspiciously well-timed or too perfectly timed to be innocent.

  • "He suddenly got sick on the day of the exam. How convenient."
    → I don't really believe him. It's too perfectly timed to be a coincidence.
  • "The security footage was deleted right before the incident. Convenient."
    → This seems suspiciously helpful for someone.

The context, or the phrase "how convenient," makes the sarcasm clear. In writing, it often appears with quotation marks around convenient to signal irony.
Register: When and Where the Word Is Used

Convenient works naturally in both formal and informal situations:

  • Formal: "Please confirm a convenient date for the appointment."
  • Informal: "The store is super convenient — it's right next to my office."
  • Professional writing: "For your convenience, instructions are included on the packaging."

It belongs to everyday vocabulary, so you can use it freely in most contexts.
Summary: The Complete Picture

Convenient describes anything — a place, time, tool, method, or situation — that:

  1. Fits your needs without requiring extra effort
  2. Saves you time or trouble
  3. Works well with your schedule, location, or circumstances
  4. Doesn't create new problems or difficulties for you

The word is about ease of fit: things fall into place without friction. The more something reduces the effort, distance, or awkwardness involved in doing something, the more convenient it is.

And in its ironic use? It captures what happens when something is too perfectly timed — conveniently good for someone in a way that raises an eyebrow.
3493:
A convent is a place where a group of nuns live together as a religious community. It refers to two closely connected things at once:

  1. The building (or complex of buildings) where nuns live
  2. The community of nuns living there

So when someone says "she entered the convent," they mean she became a nun and joined that religious community. When someone says "the convent is on the hill," they're talking about the physical building.

Nuns — women who have chosen to dedicate their entire lives to God and religious service. To become a nun, a woman takes formal vows, which are solemn, binding religious promises. These typically include:

  • Poverty — giving up personal wealth and ownership
  • Chastity — choosing a life without romantic or sexual relationships
  • Obedience — following the rules of their religious order and their superiors

Once a woman takes these vows, she becomes a full member of the convent's community. The nuns in a convent belong to a particular religious order — an organized group within the Catholic Church (or sometimes other Christian denominations) that follows a specific set of rules and traditions. Examples include the Carmelites, the Poor Clares, the Dominicans, and the Sisters of Charity.

The head or leader of a convent is usually called a Mother Superior or an Abbess, who is responsible for guiding and governing the community.
What goes on inside a convent?

Life in a convent is highly structured and revolves around two main pillars: prayer and work.

The nuns follow a daily rhythm that includes multiple sessions of communal prayer at fixed times throughout the day — early morning, midday, evening, and sometimes during the night. This practice of praying together at set hours is called the Divine Office or the Liturgy of the Hours, and it forms the backbone of convent life.

Outside of prayer, nuns also work. The nature of this work depends on the type of convent.

1. Enclosed (or cloistered) convents

In these convents, the nuns live in almost complete separation from the outside world. They rarely, if ever, leave the convent premises. Their primary purpose is contemplation — deep, devoted prayer and meditation. They believe their life of prayer benefits the world spiritually, even without going out into it. The Poor Clares and the Discalced Carmelites are well-known examples of enclosed orders.

In a cloistered convent, there is often a grille — a partition or screen — between the nuns and any visitors, maintaining a physical separation even when they do communicate with outsiders.

2. Active (or apostolic) convents

In these convents, nuns balance prayer with direct service to the wider community. They go out into the world and do practical work such as:

  • Teaching in schools
  • Nursing and caring for the sick
  • Running orphanages or shelters
  • Doing missionary work
  • Social work among the poor

The Missionaries of Charity, founded by Mother Teresa, are a famous example of an active order.
The physical structure of a convent

A convent is not just a single building — it is typically a complex that includes several spaces built to support the community's life:

  • A chapel or oratory — the central space for prayer and worship
  • Cells — small, simple, private rooms where each nun sleeps and sometimes prays alone (not prison cells; the word comes from the Latin for a small room)
  • A refectory — the communal dining hall
  • A cloister — a covered walkway forming a square around an open courtyard, often used for quiet walking and reflection; this is also where the word "cloistered" comes from
  • Gardens, a library, a kitchen, and workrooms

The design is intentional: everything is arranged to support a life of simplicity, prayer, and community.

These words are closely related and often confused:

  • Monastery: Traditionally used for a community of monks (men), though in strict usage it can apply to any enclosed religious community, male or female. In everyday speech, people tend to say "monastery" for men and "convent" for women.
  • Nunnery: An older, more literary or historical term for a convent. You'll encounter it in older literature (Shakespeare uses it), but it's rarely used today.
  • Abbey: A larger, self-governing religious house — it can be for either monks or nuns. A convent may sometimes be called an abbey if it has a certain level of independence and is led by an abbess.
  • Priory: A smaller religious house, often dependent on a larger abbey.
  • Friary: A house for friars (members of mendicant orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans).

The simplest rule: in modern usage, convent = community and home of nuns.

Because many convents historically ran schools, people in some countries (especially in Ireland, India, and parts of the UK) informally use "convent" to refer to a school run by nuns — as in "She studied at a convent" or "It's a convent school." This is a derived, informal usage rather than the core meaning, but it is widely understood and common in everyday speech.

A convent is both the community of nuns and the place where they live. It is a self-contained world built around religious vows, structured prayer, and — depending on the type — either deep contemplative solitude or active service to others. The word captures not just a building, but a whole way of life chosen by women who have committed themselves entirely to their faith.
3494: Before diving into the different meanings, here is the single idea that runs through all of them: a "convention" is something that a group of people have come to agree on together — whether that agreement is about how to behave, what to believe is normal, or the act of gathering together physically. Keep this core idea in mind and every meaning will make perfect sense.
Meaning 1: An Unspoken Rule That Society Has Agreed Upon

This is the most important and widely used meaning.

A convention is a way of doing something that most people in a group, society, or field accept and follow — not because a law forces them to, but because it has simply become the "normal" or "expected" way of doing things over time.

Nobody wrote it down in a rulebook. Nobody voted on it. People just... collectively settled on it, and now everyone follows it out of habit, respect, or social expectation.

Examples:

  • In most countries, it is a social convention to shake hands when you meet someone for the first time.
  • Starting a formal letter with "Dear Mr./Ms. [Name]" is a writing convention.
  • Wearing black to a funeral is a social convention in many Western cultures.
  • In English writing, it is a convention to put a comma after introductory phrases like "However," or "In addition,".
  • Clapping at the end of a performance is a convention — nobody is forced to, but everyone does it because it has become the accepted way to show appreciation.

The Key Point:

A convention is not a law. If you break a law, you face legal punishment. If you break a convention, you face something softer — confusion, disapproval, awkwardness, or social judgment. For example, if you show up to a funeral wearing bright red, you haven't broken any law, but you have violated a social convention, and people will react accordingly.

Conventions Can Be Field-Specific:

Different fields, professions, and communities have their own conventions.

  • Literary conventions: In stories, the hero often faces a great obstacle before winning. Villains are frequently introduced with dark, ominous music in films. These are storytelling conventions.
  • Scientific writing conventions: Scientists write in a formal, impersonal tone and use passive voice ("The experiment was conducted...") rather than saying "I did the experiment."
  • Musical conventions: In Western classical music, a symphony traditionally has four movements. This is a convention — composers can break it, but audiences expect it.
  • Business conventions: Replying to a professional email within 24–48 hours is a workplace convention.
Meaning 2: A Large Formal Gathering or Meeting

A convention is also a large organized event where people who share a common interest, profession, or purpose come together to meet, exchange ideas, discuss issues, or make decisions.

Think of it as a big, formal get-together — often with speeches, panels, exhibitions, and networking.

Examples:

  • A political party convention is where members of a political party gather to officially nominate their candidate for an election and agree on their party's goals and policies.
  • A medical convention is where doctors, researchers, and healthcare professionals gather to share new research and discoveries.
  • A comic book convention (like the famous San Diego Comic-Con) is where fans of comics, movies, and pop culture gather to celebrate shared interests, meet creators, and see new announcements.
  • A teachers' convention is where educators gather to discuss new teaching methods and curriculum changes.

The Connection to Meaning 1:

Notice the link — in both meanings, people are coming together and agreeing on something. In Meaning 1, it's an agreement about behavior or norms. In Meaning 2, it's a literal physical coming-together of people.
Meaning 3: A Formal Agreement Between Countries or Groups

In international relations and law, a convention is a formal, written agreement between two or more countries (or other official bodies) that sets out rules they all agree to follow.

It is similar to a treaty. The difference is mostly in tone and usage — a treaty tends to be a broader political agreement, while a convention usually focuses on a specific issue (human rights, warfare, the environment, trade, etc.).

Examples:

  • The Geneva Conventions are a set of international agreements that establish rules for how soldiers and civilians must be treated during war (for example, that prisoners of war must be treated humanely).
  • The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child is an agreement signed by most countries in the world, establishing the basic rights that every child is entitled to.
  • The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations sets the rules for how countries must treat each other's diplomats and embassies.

The Connection to the Core Idea:

Again, the same thread — multiple parties coming together and agreeing on something, this time officially and in writing.

Understanding how a word is different from its neighbors sharpens your understanding of it enormously.

Convention vs. Law:
A law is formally written, enforced by a government, and carries legal penalties. A social convention is informal, enforced only by social pressure and expectation. You must follow a law. You are merely expected to follow a convention.

Convention vs. Tradition:
A tradition is usually tied to history, culture, or ritual — something passed down across generations (like celebrating a holiday in a specific way). A convention is more about a practical, agreed-upon norm for how things are done. Traditions tend to feel more emotional and heritage-driven; conventions tend to feel more like practical agreements. (There is, however, significant overlap, and the two words are sometimes used interchangeably in casual speech.)

Convention vs. Rule:
A rule is explicit — it is stated clearly and is meant to be enforced. A convention is often unwritten and unspoken. In a classroom, "raise your hand before speaking" is a rule. But arriving five minutes early to an important meeting is a convention.

You will often see the phrase "by convention", which simply means "because it has been generally agreed upon and accepted as the standard way," even if there is no deep logical reason for it.

  • "In the Northern Hemisphere, maps are drawn with north at the top — but this is by convention, not because there is a "correct" direction in space."
  • "Doctors, by convention, write prescriptions in a specific format."
  • "By convention, the best man stands to the right of the groom at a wedding."

When someone breaks with convention or defies convention, it means they deliberately choose to act against what is normally expected or accepted. This phrase often carries a positive, bold, or creative connotation — as if the person is being brave or original.

  • "The architect broke with convention by designing a building with no straight walls."
  • "She defied convention by wearing a colorful dress to the black-tie event."
Summary: The Three Meanings at a Glance

Here they are in plain terms, without a table:

1. An unspoken, accepted norm of behavior — the "way things are done" in a society, culture, or field, followed out of social expectation rather than legal obligation. (Social conventions, literary conventions, professional conventions.)

2. A large organized gathering — a formal event where people with shared interests or roles come together. (A political convention, a comic-con, a medical convention.)

3. A formal international agreement — a written agreement between countries on a specific issue, similar to a treaty. (The Geneva Conventions, the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.)

The invisible thread connecting all three: people coming together and agreeing on something. Whether that "something" is a shared norm, a physical meeting, or a formal written agreement — the spirit of collective agreement is always at the heart of the word.
3495:
"Conventional" describes something that follows the widely accepted, commonly practiced, or traditionally established way of doing things. It sticks to what most people in a society, field, or group consider normal, standard, or expected.

To understand this word deeply, you first need to understand what a convention is, because "conventional" is built on that idea. A convention is an unwritten social agreement — a widely shared habit or norm that people follow, not because a law forces them to, but because "that's just how things are done." Shaking hands as a greeting is a convention. Wearing a suit to a job interview is a convention. Writing a letter with "Dear..." at the top is a convention. "Conventional" simply means something that aligns with, or conforms to, these kinds of agreed-upon standards.
The Full Range of Its Meaning

The word works across several situations, and understanding each one gives you complete mastery of it.

1. Following social norms and customs

When describing a person's lifestyle or behavior, "conventional" means they live in a way that most people would consider normal and expected — no surprises, nothing unusual.

  • "She leads a conventional life: a steady job, a house, two kids, and family dinners on Sundays."
  • "His conventional behavior made him easy to trust."

Here, the word is neutral to mildly positive. The person is simply following the mainstream path.

2. Ordinary, predictable, unoriginal

"Conventional" can also mean something that plays it too safe — that it follows the standard pattern so closely that it lacks creativity or freshness. In this sense, it carries a mildly negative flavor.

  • "The movie was entertaining, but the plot was too conventional — you could predict every twist."
  • "His designs are competent but conventional. Nothing stands out."

Notice that the word doesn't mean bad here. It means ordinary in a way that fails to surprise or impress.

3. Standard, as opposed to an alternative method

In many fields, "conventional" contrasts with something newer, alternative, or experimental. It means the traditional, mainstream approach that most people use or accept.

  • "Conventional medicine" refers to the standard treatments used by doctors — as opposed to herbal remedies, homeopathy, or other alternative approaches.
  • "Conventional farming" uses standard practices like chemical fertilizers and pesticides — as opposed to organic farming.
  • "Conventional energy" comes from coal, gas, or oil — as opposed to solar or wind.

In these cases, "conventional" is completely neutral. It just means the established, mainstream option.

4. Non-nuclear (in military contexts)

In discussions about weapons and warfare, "conventional" has a very specific technical meaning. It refers to standard weapons — guns, bombs, missiles — as opposed to nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons.

  • "The country's military relies on conventional weapons."
  • "The treaty limited the use of both conventional and nuclear forces."

This is one of the most common uses of the word, and it deserves its own explanation. "Conventional wisdom" refers to the ideas, beliefs, or conclusions that most people in a society generally accept as true — the "common knowledge" that is taken for granted.

  • "Conventional wisdom says that you should drink eight glasses of water a day."
  • "The startup succeeded by challenging conventional wisdom about how software should be sold."

The phrase is often used to set up a contrast — first stating what everyone believes, then questioning or overturning it. It doesn't mean the belief is necessarily correct; it just means it is widely held.
The Tone: Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

This is where learners often get confused, so let's settle it clearly.

"Conventional" is a chameleon. Its tone shifts depending on the context and the speaker's attitude.

It is neutral when you are simply describing something as standard or mainstream, with no judgment intended. "Conventional medicine saved his life." Nobody is criticizing or praising anything — just describing.

It is mildly positive when reliability, predictability, or social trust is valued. A conventional approach to surgery is reassuring — you want your surgeon to follow established, proven methods, not experiment on you.

It is mildly negative when the speaker values originality, boldness, or creativity. Calling a novel "conventional" from a literary critic is practically a polite insult — it means the book does nothing new or daring.

The key insight: the word itself is neutral, but the value of being conventional depends entirely on the situation. In brain surgery, conventional is good. In art, it can be limiting.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Several words are close to "conventional," but each has its own angle.

Traditional emphasizes something passed down over a long period of time, often across generations. It has a warmer, more historical feeling. A traditional recipe is one that has been made the same way for decades. A conventional recipe is simply one that follows standard, expected cooking methods. The difference is subtle but real — "traditional" looks backward at history, while "conventional" looks sideways at what the majority currently accepts.

Orthodox is stronger. It means strictly following the established rules or doctrines of a system — often used in religion, science, or medicine. An orthodox belief leaves no room for deviation. "Conventional" is softer and more flexible.

Standard is the most neutral of all. It simply means the default or normal version of something, without any social judgment. A standard procedure. "Conventional" carries a slightly stronger sense of social agreement and norm-following.

Typical means characteristic of a type or category. A typical Monday morning. "Conventional" means following accepted norms, not just being a representative example.

Understanding a word's opposite sharpens your grasp of it enormously. The clearest opposite of "conventional" is unconventional — meaning something that breaks from accepted norms, does things differently, or refuses to follow the usual path.

Other words that contrast with "conventional" include: unorthodox, radical, alternative, innovative, original, avant-garde, experimental, and revolutionary. Each one implies a departure from the standard, expected way of doing things — which is exactly what "conventional" embraces.

"Conventional" describes anything — a person, a method, a belief, an object, a style — that conforms to what is widely accepted, practiced, or expected within a given group or society. It can mean socially normal, it can mean ordinary to the point of being unexciting, it can mean the mainstream alternative to something newer or experimental, and in military language, it specifically means non-nuclear.

Its tone ranges from warm and reliable to mildly dull, depending entirely on whether the context rewards conformity or creativity. When convention is the safe, proven path, being conventional is wise. When convention is holding something back, being conventional is a flaw.

That, in full, is what "conventional" means.
3496: Conventional wisdom is any idea, belief, or explanation that most people in a society accept as true — not necessarily because it has been proven beyond doubt, but simply because it has been widely repeated, rarely challenged, and passed down over time.
Breaking Down the Two Words

To really understand the term, it helps to look at the two words separately.

"Conventional" means something that follows convention — that is, the usual, accepted, or standard way of thinking or doing things in a group or society. It's what the majority agrees on without much argument. "Conventional" often implies something old, comfortable, and unquestioned.

"Wisdom" normally means deep, reliable knowledge and good judgment gained from experience or reflection. True wisdom is usually accurate and trustworthy.

Now, here's the interesting tension: when you put these two words together, the phrase does not actually guarantee truth. "Conventional wisdom" is wisdom in name, but it is only conventional in practice — meaning it is popular and widely believed, not necessarily verified or correct.
The Core Idea, Explained Simply

Imagine that almost everyone in your neighborhood believes that drinking cold water when you have a cold will make it worse. Nobody has really studied this. Nobody proved it. But parents told children, children told friends, and friends told strangers — and eventually, nearly everyone just accepted it as true. Nobody questions it anymore because everybody believes it.

That shared, unquestioned belief — that is conventional wisdom.

It is the default answer that most people reach for when asked about a topic, without feeling the need to double-check it.
Where the Term Comes From

The phrase "conventional wisdom" was made famous by the American economist John Kenneth Galbraith in his 1958 book The Affluent Society. He used it — quite critically — to describe ideas that are accepted not because they are accurate, but because they are familiar, comfortable, and safe.

Galbraith noticed that people in politics, economics, and everyday life tend to prefer ideas that do not disturb or challenge the status quo. These comfortable, familiar ideas become the "conventional wisdom" of their time — and they can be very hard to dislodge, even when new evidence contradicts them.
How Conventional Wisdom Forms

Conventional wisdom does not appear overnight. It builds up gradually through a predictable pattern:

Step 1 — Someone says something. An idea is introduced — sometimes by an expert, sometimes by a popular figure, and sometimes just by a random person who spoke loudly and confidently.

Step 2 — It spreads. People repeat the idea to others. It appears in books, articles, speeches, casual conversations.

Step 3 — It becomes "common knowledge." After being repeated enough times, the idea stops being questioned. It enters the background of daily life as something "everyone knows."

Step 4 — It becomes invisible. The idea is now so embedded in society that people forget how it started or whether anyone ever proved it. It is simply assumed to be true. Questioning it starts to feel strange or even rude.

At this point, it has become conventional wisdom.
A Key Characteristic: It Feels Obvious

One of the most important features of conventional wisdom is that it feels obvious to the people who hold it. They don't feel like they're believing something on faith — they feel like they're just stating plain common sense.

This is what makes conventional wisdom so powerful and also so potentially dangerous. When an idea feels obvious, people stop examining it. And when people stop examining something, errors can survive for a very long time.
Examples That Make It Clear

Here are some examples of things that have been (or still are) conventional wisdom at various points in history:

Example 1 — The Earth is flat.
For most of human history, this was the default belief of ordinary people. It felt obvious — you can look around and the ground looks flat. Sailors, travelers, and common folk simply accepted it. It was conventional wisdom, not science.

Example 2 — You should eat three meals a day.
This is widely accepted as healthy fact. But in reality, historians note this pattern was largely shaped by industrial work schedules and social customs in the 19th century — not by nutritional science. It is largely conventional wisdom, not a universal biological law.

Example 3 — Ulcers are caused by stress.
For decades, the medical world accepted this as settled fact. Doctors told patients to reduce stress and change their diets. Then in 1984, two Australian scientists (Barry Marshall and Robin Warren) discovered that most ulcers are actually caused by a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori. They were initially laughed at — because they were challenging conventional wisdom. They later won a Nobel Prize.

Example 4 — Blood should be kept in the body during surgery.
For most of medical history, bloodletting — draining blood from sick patients — was considered effective treatment. Physicians across the world practiced it confidently. It was wrong, and it killed people. But for centuries, it was conventional wisdom.

Example 5 — A college degree always leads to success.
This is a widespread belief in many modern societies. It may have been more reliably true in certain decades, but in many contexts today it is an oversimplification. Still, it circulates widely as if it were an absolute truth.
When Conventional Wisdom Is Right

It would be unfair and inaccurate to say conventional wisdom is always wrong. Sometimes, a widely-held belief is widely held because it is correct. Through repeated experience, societies often stumble onto useful truths that get passed down correctly.

For example:

  • "Wash your hands before eating" — was common wisdom long before germ theory explained why it worked.
  • "Don't drink seawater when you're thirsty at sea" — sailors knew this from experience before the science of osmosis was understood.
  • "Exercise is good for your health" — broadly true, and also broadly believed.

The point is not that conventional wisdom is always false. The point is that it is not reliable proof of truth by itself. You cannot say something is true just because "everyone knows it." The validity of a belief must be checked independently.
When Conventional Wisdom Is Dangerous

Conventional wisdom becomes dangerous when:

It discourages questioning. Because the idea is "what everyone knows," raising doubts can feel socially awkward or even rebellious. This social pressure protects wrong ideas from scrutiny.

It is used to justify important decisions. When policymakers, doctors, or business leaders make major choices based on unexamined conventional wisdom, the consequences can be serious.

It serves someone's interests. Sometimes, a belief becomes "conventional wisdom" because powerful people — corporations, governments, institutions — benefit from promoting it. The idea that cigarettes were harmless was, for a time, nearly conventional wisdom in parts of society — a view that the tobacco industry spent enormous money to create and sustain.

It is mistaken for expert consensus. People often confuse conventional wisdom (popular opinion) with scientific consensus (carefully studied expert agreement). These are very different things. Scientific consensus changes slowly and is based on evidence. Conventional wisdom can change fast and is based on popularity.
Conventional Wisdom vs. Scientific Consensus

This distinction is important enough to deserve its own section.

Conventional wisdom is what most ordinary people believe. It is shaped by culture, media, repetition, and social norms. It requires no formal study or evidence.

Scientific consensus is what a large body of qualified researchers agree on after careful, repeated, peer-reviewed study. It is also not perfect — science evolves — but it is far more reliable than popular belief.

For example, that human activity is causing climate change is scientific consensus. That "we only use 10% of our brains" is conventional wisdom — and it is false.

Always be careful not to use these two concepts interchangeably.
How to Think About Conventional Wisdom in Real Life

Here is a simple mental framework you can use whenever you hear something that sounds like conventional wisdom:

Ask: "How do we know this?"
Is the belief based on careful study, or is it just something that has been repeated a lot?

Ask: "Who benefits from this belief being widespread?"
Sometimes beliefs spread because they serve the interests of powerful people or institutions.

Ask: "Has anyone checked this recently?"
Some ideas were true in one era but are outdated in another. Circumstances change.

Ask: "What is the actual evidence?"
This is the most important question. Evidence is the difference between knowledge and assumption.
A One-Paragraph Summary to Remember

Conventional wisdom is the body of ideas, beliefs, and assumptions that most people in a society accept without much questioning — not because they have been proven rigorously, but because they have been repeated so widely and for so long that they feel like obvious common sense. The term was popularized by economist John Kenneth Galbraith to describe beliefs that are comfortable and familiar, rather than necessarily correct. Conventional wisdom can sometimes be right, but it can also preserve serious errors for generations. The key insight is this: widespread belief is not the same as truth. Something being "what everybody knows" is not evidence that it is accurate — it is only evidence that it is popular. The critical thinker treats conventional wisdom as a starting point for inquiry, not as the end of it.

To converge means to come together from different starting points toward a single point, place, or outcome.

Picture two rivers flowing through separate valleys. As they travel, they gradually get closer and closer until they finally meet and flow as one. That entire process — the gradual drawing-together from different places toward one shared point — is exactly what "converge" describes.

The word always involves three things: multiple things (at least two), moving or pointing toward a common destination, from different starting places or directions.

This is the most straightforward use of the word. People, roads, rivers, or objects that physically move toward a single location from different directions are converging.

"The two highways converge just north of the city." The roads run separately and then meet.

"Reporters converged on the courthouse from across the country." They traveled from many different places, all arriving at one spot.

Notice what makes "converge" richer than a simpler word like "meet." When two people merely meet, you just know they ended up at the same place. When they converge, you picture them coming from different directions, being drawn toward the same destination. The word contains movement and direction, not just arrival.

When people start from different viewpoints but their thinking gradually arrives at the same conclusion, their ideas are said to converge.

"After years of separate research, the two scientists' theories began to converge." They approached the problem from different angles, but the evidence kept pulling them toward the same answer.

"The committee's opinions slowly converged as the meeting went on." They disagreed at first, but gradually came to see things the same way.

This is one of the most powerful uses of the word — it captures how intellectual agreement can be a process of gradual coming-together, not just a sudden snap.

Here, "converge" is extremely precise. A sequence of numbers converges when its values keep approaching one specific number — called a limit — getting steadily closer without wandering away.

Take the sequence: 1, ½, ¼, ⅛, 1/16 ...

Each term is closer to 0 than the one before. The sequence never actually reaches 0, but it approaches 0 so reliably and predictably that mathematicians say it converges to 0. The sequence has a destination it is forever moving toward.

If a sequence instead jumps around unpredictably and never settles toward any fixed value, it does the opposite — it diverges (more on that below).

Light rays converge when they bend inward and meet at a single point. A convex lens — like the one in a magnifying glass — causes parallel rays of sunlight to converge at a single spot called the focal point. That concentrated meeting point is intensely bright and hot, which is why you can use a magnifying glass to start a fire. All that scattered light is forced to converge into one point.

When separate industries, technologies, or forces blend together into one unified thing, they are said to converge.

The smartphone is one of history's most famous examples of convergence. The telephone, camera, television, music player, computer, and GPS were once entirely separate devices and industries. They converged — came together — into a single object in your pocket.

The perfect mirror image of "converge" is diverge — to move apart, to spread away from a common point in different directions.

If two roads converge ahead, they are coming together. If they diverge, they are splitting apart.

If two scientists' opinions converge, they are reaching the same conclusion. If their opinions diverge, they are moving further apart in their thinking.

Holding these two words together makes both of them permanently clear.

Convergence is usually gradual. Things converge over time or distance — they tend toward a meeting point rather than suddenly jumping there. The process matters as much as the destination.

The word always implies multiplicity. At least two things must be involved. One thing alone cannot converge — it has nowhere to come together from.

Converge often carries a sense of pull or direction. The things coming together are being drawn toward that common point — by geography, by logic, by evidence, by gravity — not just accidentally ending up there.

These are the forms of the word you will encounter:

Converge is the base verb. "The paths converge at the peak."

Converging is the present participle (ongoing action). "Converging rivers." "Converging opinions."

Converged is the past tense. "The armies converged on the fortress at dawn."

Convergence is the noun — the state or event of converging. "The convergence of two rivers." "A remarkable convergence of ideas."

Convergent is the adjective. "Convergent paths." In psychology, convergent thinking means focusing all your reasoning toward finding one single correct answer — the opposite of creative, open-ended thinking.
To converge is to come together from different starting places toward a single point — whether those "things" are roads, rivers, people, opinions, numbers, light rays, or entire industries.
3498:
Imagine two people starting their journey from opposite ends of a city, walking toward the same meeting point. They begin far apart, but with every step, they get closer to each other — until finally, they arrive at the same place. That process, that gradual coming-together, is the heart of what convergence means.

Convergence is the process or state of different things moving toward — or meeting at — a common point, idea, result, or condition.

The key ingredients are always:

  • Multiple starting points (things that are separate or different to begin with)
  • Movement or tendency toward something shared (a point, a value, a result, an agreement)
  • The outcome — either full union or a strong tendency toward it

That's it. Everything else about this word is just this same idea applied to different fields and situations.

Think of roads. If you look at a map of highways leading into a capital city, all those roads start from different towns, different directions — north, south, east, west. But they all lead to the city center. Those roads converge at the capital. The process of all of them heading toward the same destination is convergence.

Or think of rivers. Many small streams flow down a mountain in different directions, but they gradually merge into fewer, wider rivers, which eventually flow into one large river. That merging process is convergence.

Now here's something important: convergence doesn't always mean the things literally touch. It means they are heading toward the same point or becoming increasingly alike. A river that gets closer and closer to the sea but hasn't reached it yet is still undergoing convergence.

To truly understand a word, it helps to see its opposite. The opposite of convergence is divergence — when things spread apart from a common point, moving in different directions.

Think of the beam of a flashlight. If you use a focusing lens, the rays of light are pulled inward toward a single bright spot — that's convergence. If you remove the lens, the light spreads outward in all directions — that's divergence.

Convergence = coming together → ●
Divergence = spreading apart ← ● →
How It's Used in Different Areas of Life

The beauty of "convergence" is that it travels across many subjects. The core meaning never changes, but the context does.

1. Everyday & General Usage

In casual, everyday language, convergence describes situations where separate things, forces, or events happen to meet or align.

Example: "The success of the festival was due to a convergence of great weather, talented artists, and a large enthusiastic crowd."

Here, several different favorable things all came together at the same time and place — that simultaneous arrival is called a convergence.

Another example: "A convergence of evidence pointed toward the same suspect."

Multiple clues, from different directions of inquiry, all pointed to the same conclusion. They converged on an answer.

2. Technology

This is one of the most common places you'll see the word used today. Technological convergence refers to the process by which separate devices or technologies gradually merge into one.

Think about your smartphone. It is a convergence of dozens of previously separate technologies: a telephone, a camera, a music player, a map, a calculator, a calendar, a TV, a gaming device, a flashlight, and much more — all merged into a single device.

Each of those was once its own separate product. Over time, they all came together into one. That coming-together is technological convergence.

Why it matters: Industries that were once separate (telecommunications, computing, media, entertainment) are now merging, changing how companies compete and how people live. This convergence is one of the defining forces of our era.

3. Mathematics & Science (Simplified)

In math, convergence has a precise meaning: a sequence of numbers (or a process) is said to converge if it gets closer and closer to a specific value, eventually settling on it (or approaching it without limit).

Imagine you are guessing a number. Your first guess is 10. Then 5. Then 2.5. Then 1.25. Then 0.625... Each guess is getting closer and closer to 0. This series of guesses is converging toward zero. The "destination" value (in this case, zero) is called the limit.

The opposite — a sequence that keeps growing without ever settling, like 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32... — is said to diverge.

This concept is foundational in calculus, physics, engineering, and computer science — anywhere you need to know whether a process or calculation will eventually "settle down" into a stable answer, or whether it will spiral out of control forever.

4. Biology (Convergent Evolution)

In biology, convergence (often called "convergent evolution") describes a remarkable phenomenon: completely unrelated species independently evolving the same feature or ability, because they face the same environmental challenges.

The classic example is the shape of a dolphin, a shark, and an extinct marine reptile called an ichthyosaur. These three creatures are not closely related at all — one is a mammal, one is a fish, one is a reptile. Yet all three evolved the same streamlined, torpedo-like body shape, because it is the most effective design for swimming fast through water. Nature "discovered" the same solution three times, independently.

That independent arriving at the same solution, from very different starting points, is biological convergence.

5. Economics & Politics

In economics, convergence refers to the idea that poorer economies tend to grow faster than richer ones, and over time, their income levels get closer together — they converge toward a similar standard of living.

In politics and public debate, convergence describes a situation where opposing groups or parties move closer together in their views or policies, narrowing the gap between them.

Example: "After years of debate, the two political parties showed surprising convergence on the issue of infrastructure spending."

6. Optics & Physics

In optics (the science of light), convergence refers to light rays bending toward each other to meet at a single point called the focal point. A convex (outward-curving) lens achieves this. When you use a magnifying glass to focus sunlight onto a single spot on a piece of paper to burn it, you are witnessing convergence — all those parallel rays of sunlight bent inward to meet at a single, intensely bright point.

1. Convergence implies process, not just a result.
Convergence is about the journey of coming together, not just the final point. When scientists say two measurements are "showing convergence," they mean the gap between them is shrinking over time — they may not have met yet, but the trend is clearly toward meeting.

2. Convergence can be complete or partial.
Things can fully converge (meet at one exact point) or they can tend toward convergence (get closer and closer without necessarily reaching the same point). Both situations are called convergence.

3. Convergence carries a neutral tone, but context gives it a positive or negative feel.
By itself, convergence is a neutral, descriptive word. But depending on context, it can feel positive ("convergence of support from all political parties") or worrying ("a convergence of crises — economic, environmental, and social — all at once").

4. Convergence often implies diversity at the start.
The word subtly carries the idea that the things converging were different or separate to begin with. The more different the origins, the more striking the convergence. This is what makes convergent evolution so fascinating — it's not just that two similar animals look alike, it's that they started from completely different ancestors and still arrived at the same design.
A Unifying Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear the word convergence, ask yourself:

  • What are the separate things?
  • What is the common point they are moving toward?
  • Is this a physical meeting, a blending of ideas, a mathematical settling, or something else?

Answer those three questions, and you will understand exactly what is being said — in any field, in any sentence.

The word always means the same thing at its core: separate things, coming together.

Conversant means well-acquainted with something — familiar enough with a subject to understand it, work with it, and talk about it in a knowledgeable way.

It describes a person who has a solid, practical grasp of something. Not someone who has merely heard of it, and not necessarily a deep expert — but someone who knows it well enough to engage with it confidently.
The Level of Knowledge It Implies

This is the most important thing to understand about this word, so pay close attention.

Think of knowledge as a scale:

Unaware → Heard of it → Familiar → Conversant → Proficient → Expert

Being conversant sits past casual familiarity but before deep expertise. It means you know enough to understand the subject when it comes up, discuss it sensibly, ask and answer questions about it, and handle it without confusion — but it doesn't claim that you are a master of it.

Think of it as the level where you can hold your own on the topic. You won't be lost. You won't be clueless. But you're not necessarily the foremost authority either.

For example:

  • A history student who has studied the French Revolution thoroughly is conversant with it — they can discuss causes, key figures, and consequences comfortably.
  • A doctor who has studied enough law to understand medical malpractice procedures is conversant with legal matters in that area.
  • Someone who has used spreadsheet software regularly for years is conversant with it.
The Preposition That Goes With It

Conversant is almost always followed by the word "with".

You are conversant with something — not in, not about, not of.

✅ "She is conversant with modern data analysis techniques."
✅ "He is conversant with the terms of the contract."
❌ "She is conversant in data analysis." ← possible but less standard
❌ "He is conversant about the contract." ← incorrect

Think of it like this: you are with the subject — side by side with it, comfortable in its company, on familiar terms with it.

Let's look at several examples across different contexts so the word really sinks in:

  • "The new employee was conversant with the company's accounting software, so she needed very little training."
    She already knew the software well enough to use it without hand-holding.
  • "As a foreign policy advisor, he must be conversant with the political situations of dozens of countries."
    His job requires him to have solid, working knowledge of many countries' politics.
  • "The doctor was conversant with the legal procedures involved in obtaining patient consent."
    She wasn't a lawyer, but she knew enough about those procedures to handle them correctly.
  • "Not everyone on the team is conversant with the new regulations, so we need a training session."
    Some team members lack the necessary familiarity — they're not up to speed yet.
  • "To work in international finance, you need to be conversant with foreign exchange markets."
    You need a real, working knowledge — not just a surface awareness.

Getting clear on what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does mean.

  • It does NOT mean "expert." If someone is conversant with tax law, they are not necessarily a tax lawyer or an authority. They simply know it well enough to work with it.
  • It does NOT mean just "aware of." Saying "I've heard of blockchain technology" is not being conversant with it. Conversant implies you actually know it — you've engaged with it enough to understand how it works.
  • It does NOT refer to your personality or how talkative you are. A common beginner mistake is to think this word is related to being conversational (as in, chatty or friendly to talk to). It is not. It is purely about your knowledge and familiarity with a subject. The two words look similar but mean very different things.

Conversant is a formal, educated word. You'll encounter it most in professional writing, academic contexts, job descriptions, and formal speech — not in casual, everyday conversation.

For example, a job posting might say:

"The ideal candidate will be conversant with international trade law and supply chain logistics."

In everyday casual speech, people would more likely say "familiar with" or "knows their way around" — but in formal contexts, conversant with is precise and carries a professional weight.

Whenever you're unsure if conversant is the right word to use, ask yourself:

"Does this person know this subject well enough to work with it and discuss it intelligently — even if they're not an expert?"

If yes — conversant is your word.
